sections.history: Tirukazhippalai is a Shaiva shrine of the Chola country, set on the northern bank of the Kollidam, the river that carries the waters of the Kaveri down to the sea near Chidambaram. It is a Paadal Petra Sthalam, praised in the Tevaram by Sambandar, Appar and Sundarar, and the later poet Arunagirinathar also remembered it in verse. The first temple stood close to the riverbank, and tradition holds that floods damaged it. Palvannanathar and the attendant deities were then established in a new temple at Sivapuri, beside Tirunelvoyal and within easy reach of Chidambaram. The worship that began in the old sanctuary has continued unbroken in the new one.
sections.architecture: The temple is modest in scale, a compact complex of about an acre enclosed by concentric rectangular walls and entered beneath a three-tiered rajagopuram. The sanctum holds the Shiva linga of Palvannanathar, while the goddess Vedanayaki is honoured in her own shrine beside the mandapam, facing south. Around the prakaram stand shrines to Surya, Vinayaka, Subramanya, Vishnu, Mahalakshmi, the Navagrahas and Chandra, and a Kala Bhairava whose image is said to resemble the Bhairava of Varanasi, so that the temple is also known as a place of Bhairava worship. The vilva is the sacred tree, and the Kollidam itself serves as the temple's holy water.
sections.legends: The Lord's name tells the story. The sage Kapilar, in a forest on the river's edge, shaped a lingam from white sand and set it up for worship. A king's horse passing that way struck it with its hoof and left a mark. Coming back to worship, the sage found the wound and, thinking the lingam unfit, began to fashion another. Then Shiva and Parvati appeared and stayed his hand. They told him that the sand of the place was white because the celestial cow Kamadhenu had once poured her milk over all of it, and that the lingam, touched by that milk, was already made holy. The Lord took the name Palvannanathar, the Lord of the milk-white hue. Devotees say that the milk offered over the image in worship is drawn into it. Tellers differ on the fate of the marked lingam, but not on the meaning: what has been hallowed is not diminished by a wound.
sections.festivals: The principal festival is the Brahmotsavam in the Tamil month of Vaikasi (May–June), when the deities are borne out in procession and the town gathers for the days of worship. Maha Shivaratri and the monthly Pradosham are observed as at every Shiva temple, and devotees of Kala Bhairava keep the shrine with special attention on his sacred days. Confirm dates locally, as they follow the Tamil calendar.
sections.experience: Tirukazhippalai is a quiet temple, best approached without hurry. Pause beneath the gopuram, come to the sanctum of Palvannanathar, and let the story of the milk-white Lord settle before turning to Vedanayaki in her south-facing shrine. Many devotees bring milk for the Lord's abhishekam, a gesture that carries the whole meaning of the place. Take time too at the Kala Bhairava shrine in the prakaram. Because the temple stands beside Tirunelvoyal, near Chidambaram, it pairs naturally with a visit to the nearby sung shrines of the area.

visit.timings: Typically open in the morning and again from late afternoon into the evening, with a midday closure; hours vary on festival days, so confirm locally.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected, with shoulders and knees covered: dhoti or trousers for men; saree, salwar kameez or a long skirt for women. Footwear is removed before entering the temple.
visit.photography: Photography is usually allowed in the outer courtyards but not within the sanctum. Please ask the temple staff before photographing priests or rituals.
visit.gettingThere: The temple stands at Sivapuri, beside Tirunelvoyal, about 4 km from the Chidambaram bus stand on the Kavarapattu route, in Cuddalore district. Chidambaram has the nearest railway station and is well served by buses from Chennai, Puducherry and Kumbakonam. Chennai is the principal airport, a little over 200 km away by road.
